Blue Origin Advances LC-36 Rebuild for Year-End New Glenn Return to Flight
candidates.raw_excerpt: Four months after Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket exploded on the launch pad, the company continues to show quick progress as it attempts to return to flight before year-end. With roughly three months remaining, attention is focused on whether reconstruction of Launch Complex-36 (LC-36) is approaching the halfway mark. LC-36 Reconstruction The most visually apparent changes involve the pad towers. Before the explosion, two structures stood: the support tower and the lightning tower. The blast toppled the lightning tower and caused structural damage to the support tower, bending beams. Blue Origin also lost its large transporter-erector, which previously supplied propellants and other commodities to the vehicle. To accelerate return-to-flight efforts, the company shifted from horizontal to vertical integration, eliminating the transporter-erector and relying solely on the support tower. This approach mirrors operations used with SpaceX’s Starship. The change requires not only repairs to the support tower but also upgrades so that it can transfer super-cold cryogenic propellant from the tank farm to the vehicle. According to CEO Dave Limp, the fastest method was to destack the majority of the modules, repair and upgrade them on the ground in parallel, and then reassemble the tower. Blue Origin teams have pursued that work since the summer, adding new floors and guard rails for worker access along with the ground support equipment needed to move cryogenic propellant up the tower. That phase is now wrapping up. Over the past few days, the first and second modules have returned to the tower and been stacked by one of the many cranes operating at LC-36. candidates.title: This Graph of Data Center Spending Compared to All Other Construction Will Give You Chills
candidates.raw_excerpt: Against all odds, the US economy continues to grow at a record-setting pace. Yet as new economic data shows, that growth is anything but healthy, and predicated almost entirely on the AI boom. A new essay by podcaster and writer Derek Thompson takes a look at key economic metrics surrounding AI in 2026. Among the most striking is a bar graph showing growth in construction spending, a key indicator of economic stability. Using data from Harvard Kennedy School economist Jason Furman, Thompson shows that growth in data center construction has exploded this year, while all but one other category has regressed. By the numbers, data center construction has grown at a rate of 64.5 percent in the most recent year, while new energy infrastructure has grown by 4.1 percent to keep pace — since demand is growing for electricity to power the AI boom. Everything else has collapsed: multi-family home building fell by 5.6 percent, while healthcare and commercial retail construction both tumbled by 10.1 percent. New educational construction tumbled by 12.6 percent, while manufacturing — supposedly a key target for the Trump administration — has collapsed, shrinking nearly 24 percent from 2025 to 2026. Thompson is perhaps best known for his “abundance” theory, a deregulation-brained policy agenda with roots in neoliberal economic thought. But if there’s any abundance to be had in the US economy at the moment, it’s clearly coming on the back of AI — and with investors growing increasingly skeptical over the sustainability of AI spending, it could only be a matter of time before data center spending tumbles back down to Earth. candidates.title: Chinese scientists identify gene linked to brain evolution
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Recently, Chinese researchers have found experimental evidence that the gene CCNB1IP1 plays a key role in brain development and may have contributed to the evolution of human intelligence. Experiments in mice showed that increasing the gene's expression to human levels promoted cortical folding and improved learning and memory, offering new insights into the genetic mechanisms underlying brain evolution.

The study was led by researchers at the Kunming Institute of Zoology under the Chinese Academy of Sciences. By comparing brain development across species, the team investigated the role of CCNB1IP1 in the evolution of the brain.

One distinctive feature of the human brain is its highly folded cerebral cortex, the outer layer involved in many higher cognitive functions. These folds, known as gyri and sulci, increase the cortex's surface area while allowing it to fit within the limited space of the skull. Although cortical folding is associated with brain expansion and cognitive evolution, the degree of folding alone does not determine intelligence.

The researchers found that CCNB1IP1 expression was associated with the expansion and folding of the cerebral cortex during primate evolution. When they increased the gene's expression in mice to human levels, the animals developed folds in their otherwise smooth cerebral cortex and performed better in learning and memory tests. The findings provide further evidence of a link between CCNB1IP1, cortical development and cognitive function, offering new clues to the genetic mechanisms that may have shaped the evolution of the human brain.

candidates.title: Hot Take: How technology helps a city act before complaints arrive
candidates.raw_excerpt:
How can a city hear its people before they even speak? In Beijing, the answer starts with a phone number: 12345.

Over the past seven years, this hotline has handled 180 million requests from residents and businesses, with resolution and satisfaction rates both above 97%. But the real story is not just the calls that come in. It is what technology does with the information.

Every day, AI-powered systems sift through the data, grouping complaints by keyword, location and urgency and generating heat maps that show where the city is struggling. Analysts use these patterns to anticipate emerging problems: which neighborhoods repeatedly experience issues, which disputes peak in certain months and which types of complaints arrive in waves.

A single case tells you little; the data can reveal much more. For example, if elevator complaints in one district keep climbing, maintenance or renewal needs may be mounting.

The data does not just record the past. It points to the future.

This is where "One Topic a Month" begins.

Every month, algorithms identify a high-frequency problem in the data and bring it to the attention of a municipal department. Three levels of government work together. The goal is not to resolve a single case, but to address an entire category of problems.

Yet technology alone cannot govern a city.

Volunteer "lane managers" walk the alleys, spotting problems before they grow. Residents, businesses and community workers all become part of the early-warning system, providing eyes and ears that no algorithm can replace.

The result is a city that no longer waits for the phone to ring.

Astrolight upgraded the ground station to its OGS-2.5 model for the PeakSat mission. Astrolight’s team in Lithuania has operated both systems remotely. The company reports that ATLAS-1 is currently transmitting data at 1 Gbps, while link budget margins indicate that the system could support rates of up to 10 Gbps. Both ATLAS-1 and OGS-2.5 achieved first light during the satellite’s first active pass over the ground station. The systems operated autonomously on a pre-scheduled basis at both ends of the link by the third pass. “The next step for laser communications is making them routine for satellite operators, with high-capacity links that can be deployed and operated remotely with minimal operational oversight. Proving that our space and ground systems have this capability brings us closer to making optical connectivity practical for commercial missions at scale,” Dalius Petrulionis, CTO and co-founder of Astrolight, said in a statement.
